description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

items.title: Washington puts federal cyber teams inside Texas water plants as July’s attacks are pinned at 30-plus Minnesota systems
items.content_text: The White House launched Project Watershed 250 on 31 August, a six-month pilot that places federal, state and vendor cyber teams inside Texas water utilities at no cost to the operator, with EPA and CISA as federal partners and Texas Cyber Command running red-team exercises against live utility networks. Officials say it is not a reaction to the July attacks, but the timing tells its own story: those intrusions reached more than 100 internet-exposed water systems, and Minnesota alone has now confirmed more than 30 affected community systems, with one city’s well and treatment plant shut down outright and two more forced to manual operation. For OT defenders the significance is not the funding. It is that the federal answer to internet-exposed PLCs is now an external red team, and the findings will set the template every other sector gets measured against.

items.title: The water campaign, quantified: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
items.content_text: July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has now put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, with targeting reported across at least a dozen states including Minnesota, Michigan, South Dakota, Georgia, New Jersey and Alabama. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though supply was not widely interrupted. In some intrusions actors modified PLCs to disable shutdown processes and alarms, allowing unsafe conditions to develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was in nobody’s asset register.

items.title: A water-sector PLC maker was ransomed, and roughly 200 of its SCADA systems are reachable from the internet
items.content_text: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are nearly 850,000 stolen files totalling about 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation including system diagrams. The FBI has told the company it assesses the intrusion as opportunistic rather than targeted, and no manipulation of any customer’s control system has been reported. The number that should hold a water operator’s attention is a separate one: roughly 200 SCADAview CSX systems across US states are reachable from the public internet — the same exposure pattern that carried July’s campaign into more than 100 water systems.

items.title: The FBI seized the platform China used to hide inside other people’s routers — and the Department of Energy was on the target list
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures of the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group tracked as QTFY and operated out of Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company. The mechanics matter more to OT than the indictment does. QScan sweeps the internet and automatically compromises thousands of IoT and embedded devices; QTRouter then chains those devices, commercial proxy services and leased servers into an obfuscation network that hides where an intrusion actually originates. Court documents describe QTFY selling that capability on to the Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army, across roughly eight years of activity. Named targets include the Department of Energy, NASA, the Federal Reserve, HHS, NIH and the US Senate. Black Lotus Labs calls the arrangement a quartermaster model — reconnaissance, proxy orchestration and routing sold as a service.

items.title: Congress’s own analysts say the water sector still has no enforceable cyber floor — five weeks after plants went manual
items.content_text: The Congressional Research Service has published an assessment of federal water-sector cyber protections in the wake of July’s attacks, and its finding is uncomfortable for anyone hoping the incident wave would be self-correcting: there is still no enforceable baseline cybersecurity requirement for community water systems, EPA’s 2023 attempt to fold cyber into sanitary surveys was withdrawn after litigation, and America’s Water Infrastructure Act risk assessments neither mandate controls nor are verified. The operational reality it is measuring against is now documented in detail: more than 30 Minnesota community systems hit on 26–27 July, Braham’s well and treatment plant temporarily shut down after computerised control was disabled, Plymouth and South St. Paul running manually, and Maple Plain declaring a local state of emergency. Roughly 150,000 US systems, most of them small, sit under that voluntary regime.

items.title: Day nine at Boston Scientific: plants still disrupted by a breach that never reached a controller
items.content_text: Twelve days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific still has no full restoration date. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping remain disrupted, with EDI and GHX orders queuing unfulfilled. The company’s 30 August update states that investigators have found no signs of malicious activity in its environment since detection, that the unauthorised access appears confined to certain on-premise systems rather than cloud, and that it hoped to resume shipping at least some products this week. CrowdStrike and other responders remain engaged. Implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring are unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no group has credibly claimed it. For OT defenders the lesson is unchanged and getting louder: an enterprise-side compromise that never touched a PLC has now disrupted production for the better part of a fortnight.

items.title: NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week.

items.title: A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
items.content_text: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable.

items.title: A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC.

items.title: Fire Ant moved off hypervisors and onto the routers, TACACS servers and jump hosts that OT trusts by default
items.content_text: Sygnia has published new research on Fire Ant, the China-nexus cluster it first documented in 2025 against virtualisation infrastructure. Through 2026 the actor shifted target class: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts, held with long-lived implants, custom SSH backdoors, Medusa-family rootkit components and packet-triggered backdoors. The objective is not the compromised box. Sygnia describes the actor using that layer as a platform — harvesting administrator credentials as they pass through authentication, collecting traffic, and mapping reachability into connected high-value environments including critical infrastructure. It also suppressed router logging and altered command output, so no single telemetry source could reconstruct events. Sygnia assesses substantial overlap with the publicly reported UNC3886 tradecraft. For OT this is the bridge problem stated plainly: the routing and authentication plane your plant inherits from IT is a path in, and it is rarely instrumented like one.

items.title: SonicWall found attackers already inside its own remote-access gateway — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window.

items.title: PaperCut attacks moved from scanning to human operators pivoting inside networks, and CISA set a 14 September deadline
items.content_text: The PaperCut NG/MF print-management flaws that the vendor first warned about on 27 August have escalated sharply. Exposure-management firm WatchTowr reports that activity has shifted from exploratory probing to real exploitation with hands-on-keyboard interaction, including tradecraft aimed specifically at pivoting from external to internal networks, and payloads keyed so only the original attacker can reuse the access — behaviour it associates with initial-access brokers. Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-82078 and CVE-2026-81578, are being chained by unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and execute code; PaperCut issued two emergency patches after the first was bypassed and is still working on a consolidated release. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 31 August with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. ShadowServer counts more than 1,000 instances exposed to the internet. Print servers rarely appear on an OT risk register, yet they hold domain credentials and reach nearly every subnet in a plant.

items.title: Five federal agencies say attackers are mapping Siemens S7 controllers with AI-written tools dressed as monitoring software
items.content_text: NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August describing an active threat to Siemens S7 series programmable logic controllers in US critical infrastructure. The agencies say actors are using internet scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye to locate exposed or poorly protected S7 devices, then running AI-generated exploitation scripts presented as legitimate OT monitoring tools. The scripts are built on the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 libraries, which speak S7comm natively — so the traffic looks like ordinary engineering activity. Coverage spans the full line from S7-200 through the S7-1500 F-series safety controllers, and the agencies name critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture and commercial facilities as the most affected sectors. The assessed stage is reconnaissance and capability development, not confirmed manipulation.

items.title: Attackers are minting themselves admin tokens on Artifactory — the box a lot of plants stage firmware and engineering software from
items.content_text: JFrog disclosed CVE-2026-82329 on 28 August: an improper-authentication flaw that, in a default configuration, lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access reach the platform as an administrator. Reporting on 1 September describes exploitation in the wild within days of disclosure, with attackers generating administrator tokens and enumerating users, groups, credential sets and federated access topology. The OT relevance is not the product itself but what it holds. Artifactory is where a great many organisations stage the binaries that end up on plant floors — vendor firmware bundles, HMI and historian installers, container images for edge and IIoT gateways, engineering-workstation packages. Administrative control of that repository is the ability to alter what your change process will later install on a controller, having already passed the point at which anyone was checking. There is no confirmed OT compromise tied to this campaign at time of writing.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04).

items.title: Eleven KEV additions in eight days — decade-old server bugs, and a print server that reaches everywhere
items.content_text: CISA catalogued eleven actively exploited vulnerabilities between 24 August and 31 August. The 26 August tranche of six is instructive in composition: alongside the Citrix NetScaler flaw sit CVE-2015-3246 in Red Hat libuser, CVE-2015-5287 in Red Hat’s automatic bug reporting tool, CVE-2019-1068 in Microsoft SQL Server, CVE-2021-23758 in Ajax.NET Professional and CVE-2022-0995, a Linux kernel out-of-bounds write. On 27 August came CVE-2023-49105 in ownCloud, a Linux kernel issue tracked as CVE-2026-53362, and CVE-2026-66384 in JFrog Artifactory. The newest pair, added 31 August, are the ones to look at first: CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 in PaperCut NG/MF, a missing-authentication flaw chained with unsafe reflection to give an unauthenticated attacker code execution in the print server’s process context. Print management is exactly the kind of shared service that sits on a flat corporate segment with routes into plant networks, and the federal remediation date is 14 September.

items.title: The Coast Guard now has a single office that owns maritime cyber enforcement — expect the inspections to sharpen
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has stood up an Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy as the central authority for cyber policy across the Marine Transportation System, sitting under the Director of Inspections and Compliance. Its remit covers developing domestic policy for the cyber safety of ports, vessels and facilities, contributing to international standards, and — the line that matters operationally — directing a coordinated cybersecurity compliance and enforcement strategy. It also becomes the Coast Guard’s primary liaison to industry. For operators already working through the maritime cyber rule that entered force in 2025, this is the organisational signal that the discretionary phase is ending: a single office owning both policy and enforcement usually means more consistent inspection questions and less regional variation in how a deficiency gets written up.

items.title: In nine days, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process.

items.title: A national emergency over foreign grid equipment — and it reaches the firmware, not just the transformer
items.content_text: On 26 August the President signed Executive Order 14420, declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act with respect to foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. The order covers high-voltage infrastructure at or above 69 kV — transformers, inverters, generators and battery energy storage — and explicitly extends to associated software, firmware and remote-access capability. It prohibits transactions initiated after 26 August involving acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of covered equipment tied to designated foreign entities where the transaction poses a sabotage or disruption risk, and directs the Department of Energy to issue implementing rules within 120 days. Those rules may condition the continued operation of equipment already energised, and potentially require removal. For utilities this becomes a supply-chain compliance layer on top of NERC CIP-013, and it lands on a provenance record most operators do not have.

items.title: The standards body and the vendor coalition just signed the same paper — and both want 62443 to be the one rulebook
items.content_text: The International Society of Automation and the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition signed a memorandum of understanding on 1 September to work jointly on OT cybersecurity awareness, shared strategic issues and technical engagement between their memberships, with the stated aim of driving wider implementation and formal recognition of ISA/IEC 62443. It follows an OTCC position paper arguing for a single horizontal OT security standard in place of the current patchwork of sector-specific mandates, and it lands while the same coalition is pressing CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive setting baseline OT controls after the July water intrusions. An MOU changes nothing on a plant floor by itself. What it signals is the direction regulators are being pushed: if the harmonisation argument wins, the sector rules arriving over the next two years get written against 62443 rather than against each other, and operators who have already mapped their programme to it stop re-evidencing the same controls for every regulator.
